newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU Presidency seeks delay in cereals aid cut.
newsitem.headline: EU Presidency seeks delay in cereals aid cut.

text.p: The Irish EU Presidency proposed on Tuesday to shelve a proposal to cut cereals set-aside payments by 27 percent aimed at funding a beef market support package.

"The (Farm ministers') Council believes that any adjustment in expenditure...should be dealt with in parallel with the drafting of the budget," Ireland said in a compromise paper presented to farm ministers.

The European Commission had proposed in July cutting cereals set-aside to help finance a package of measures to cut beef output and compensate farmers following a sharp drop in beef demand due to a health scare over mad cow disease.
The Commission had proposed cutting cereals set-aside payments to 50.37 Ecus a tonne, from 68.83 Ecus. Cereals aid would also be cut to 50.37 Ecus a tonne, from 54.34 Ecus.
The Irish EU Presidency said it backed the Commission's proposal to help fund 1997 beef support measures by delaying advanced payments to oilseed farmers until 1998.
But a final decision can only be taken after the EU Parliament has given its opinion.
The Irish EU Presidency also urged the Commission to propose further financial aid for the beef and veal industry to compensate for losses due to the mad cow crisis.
"Such proposals will take account of the available financial resources," it added.
Under the compromise, the beef intervention ceiling for 1996 would be reduced to 550,000 tonnes, from the original proposal of 720,000 tonnes.
A German demand for EU aid for the early marketing of male calves up to 90 kg weight would be combined with a Commission scheme to slaughter new born male calves from dairy herds.
National ceilings on the number of male cattle eligible for EU aid payments would be cut for all member states, except Spain.
The proposed single premium for bulls would be increased by around 20 percent to 130 Ecus per head. Previously two payments were made.
A Commission spokesman said the Presidency compromise was broadly acceptable and respected financial constraints.
EU farm ministers were due shortly to give their initial reactions though an eventual agreement was still a long way off, EU officials said.
